References

On this page

Squirt flow in a cracked rock: dispersion and attenuation ​

The whole page as one script

Every block of this page, in order, is scripts/106_squirt_dispersion.jl. From a clone of the repository, julia --project=docs -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' once, then julia scripts/106_squirt_dispersion.jl, runs it end to end.

Before this page

Levin's theorem, §5, which derives the stiffness of a solid whose cracks hold a fluid, sealed, connected or exchanging it; Poromechanics and Seismic signatures, which give the syntax; and the Plane waves of TensND.

A wave that crosses a saturated cracked rock compresses some cracks more than others. At ultrasonic frequencies the fluid has no time to move: each crack keeps its own pressure. At seismic frequencies it flows from crack to crack until the pressure is uniform. The two stiffnesses differ, and the velocities measured in the laboratory are not those of the field. This page computes the two limits for the three crack arrangements of Guéguen and Sarout, against their closed forms, then the velocity and the attenuation at every frequency in between, which the exchange law of Jakobsen and Chapman gives.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization
using TensND
using LinearAlgebra
using JSON
using Printf
using Plots
gr()

The rock and its cracks ​

The solid is isotropic, of Young modulus and Poisson ratio ; the fluid is water, of bulk modulus . The values are those of all the figures of the article:

julia
literature(key) = JSON.parsefile(joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", key * ".json"))
const paper = literature("gueguen2011")
quantity(name) = paper["quantities"][name]["value"]
const E₀, ν₀, k_f = quantity("E0"), quantity("nu0"), quantity("Kf")     ## GPa
const ρ_s, ρ_f = quantity("rho_s") / 1000, quantity("rho_f") / 1000    ## g/cm³: velocities in km/s
Data read above: data/literature/gueguen2011.json 14 quantities

Guéguen, Yves, Sarout, Joël (2011). Characteristics of anisotropy and dispersion in cracked medium. Tectonophysics 503(1-2), 165-172. doi:10.1016/j.tecto.2010.09.021

Read in Section 3 and caption of Fig. 1 (p. 168), eq. (13) (p. 168), section 3.2 (p. 171), eqs (5)-(10) (p. 167), eq. (14) (p. 171) checked against the source

Transcribed from the published article (PDF), on rendered page images; every value compared with the page image

The parameters are those of all the figures of the article (p. 168, repeated in the caption of Fig. 1). The ranges of crack density and aspect ratio are those of panels a-c of Figs 2-5. The dispersion is eq. (13), the difference of the high- and low-frequency velocities of one wave divided by its velocity in the uncracked solid. The S-wave dispersion and the ratio of the P- and S-wave dispersions are quoted in the text of section 3.2 (p. 171) for randomly oriented cracks; the article computes the velocities with the density of the solid, eq. (17). The crack density is rho = N a^3/V, eq. (3), and the aspect ratio xi is the ratio of the half-opening to the radius of a crack.

Quantities

namevaluedescriptionwhere
E070.0 GPaYoung modulus of the uncracked solid. Section 3, p. 168; caption of Fig. 1
nu00.27Poisson ratio of the uncracked solid. Section 3, p. 168; caption of Fig. 1
Kf2.3 GPaBulk modulus of the pore fluid (water). Section 3, p. 168; caption of Fig. 1
rho_s2800.0 kg/m^3Mass density of the solid. Section 3, p. 168; caption of Fig. 1
rho_f1000.0 kg/m^3Mass density of the fluid. Section 3, p. 168; caption of Fig. 1
crack_density_max0.5Largest crack density of the curves against the crack density (from 0). Section 3, p. 168; panels a and b of Figs 2-5
aspect_ratio_a0.001Aspect ratio of the cracks in the curves against the crack density, panel a. Section 3, p. 168; panel a of Figs 2-5
aspect_ratio_b0.01Aspect ratio of the cracks in the curves against the crack density, panel b. Section 3, p. 168; panel b of Figs 2-5
aspect_ratio_min0.0001Smallest aspect ratio of the curves against the aspect ratio. Section 3, p. 168; panel c of Figs 2-5
aspect_ratio_max0.1Largest aspect ratio of the curves against the aspect ratio. Section 3, p. 168; panel c of Figs 2-5
crack_density_c0.3Crack density of the curves against the aspect ratio. Section 3, p. 168; panel c of Figs 2-5
dispersion_S_random0.05Dispersion of the S waves, eq. (13), for randomly oriented cracks of aspect ratio 1e-3 at the crack density 0.3. Section 3.2, p. 171 ("close to 5.10^-2")
dispersion_ratio_PS_random0.4Ratio of the P-wave dispersion to the S-wave dispersion for randomly oriented cracks. Section 3.2, p. 171 ("Delta V_P = 0.4 Delta V_S", approximate)
gamma_slope_printed_approx1.1Approximate value printed for the ratio of Thomsen's gamma to the crack density, dry aligned cracks. Eq. (14), p. 171

Notes

  • Eq. (14) prints gamma = 8(1 - nu0) alpha33 / (3(1 - 2 nu0)), followed by the approximate value 1.1 alpha33; the fraction printed gives 4.2 at nu0 = 0.27, while 8(1 - nu0)/(3(2 - nu0)) gives 1.125. The latter follows from eq. (2) of the same article.
  • Section 3 gives the range of the fluid bulk modulus of panel d of Figs 2-5 as [1e-4, 1e1] MPa while the captions and the axes give it in GPa; panel d is not used here.

The file data/literature/gueguen2011.json on GitHub, at the commit this page was built from.

The cracks are identical oblate spheroids of radius and aspect ratio (half-opening over radius). cracks in the volume have the crack density   ( in the article) and occupy the volume fraction    . The article treats them in the non-interacting approximation in compliance: each crack adds to the compliance of the solid what it would add alone in the solid under the remote stress. This is the stress-driven dilute scheme, DiluteDual.

The pressure of a fluid sealed in cracks of one normal is one number. Cracks of different normals carry different pressures, and the flow between them is what disperses the waves. Each orientation is therefore a phase of its own, with its own pressure: a single phase averaged over the orientations would hold one pressure only. A set of cracks is given by its normals , each family with the density ; the Euler angles of Spheroid are the inclination of the axis on and its azimuth.

julia
const C₀ = TensISO{3}(E₀ / (1 - 2ν₀), E₀ / (1 + ν₀))              ## 3k₀ 𝕁 + 2μ₀ 𝕂
const k₀, μ₀ = bulk_shear(C₀)
axis_angles(n) = (acos(n[3]), atan(n[2], n[1]), 0.0)
function cracked_rock(normals, ε, ξ)
    rve = RVE()
    add_phase!(rve, :solid, Ellipsoid(1.0), Dict(:C => C₀, :ρ => ρ_s); fraction = :rest)
    families = [Symbol(:cracks, i) for i in eachindex(normals)]
    for (family, n) in zip(families, normals)
        crack = Spheroid(ξ; euler_angles = axis_angles(n))
        add_phase!(rve, family, crack, Dict(:C => 0 * C₀, :ρ => ρ_f); fraction = 4π / 3 * ε * ξ / length(normals))
    end
    return rve, families
end

squirt_flow gives the complex stiffness of the saturated rock at the dimensionless frequency , being the relaxation time of the flow between cracks (Levin's theorem, §5). At   no fluid moves and the cracks are sealed: the unrelaxed, high-frequency stiffness. At   the pressure is uniform: the relaxed stiffness of Brown and Korringa, the low-frequency one. The stiffness of the fluid phases in the cell is ignored: k_f replaces it.

julia
saturated(rve, families, ωτ) = squirt_flow(rve, DiluteDual(), ωτ; fluid = families, k_f).stiffness
high(cell) = saturated(cell..., Inf)
low(cell) = saturated(cell..., 0.0)

The two limits are real; their imaginary parts, zero, are dropped before the velocities are computed by plane_waves, with the density of the rock,    , from average_density:

julia
real_stiffness(C) = Tens(real.(canonical_components(C)))
velocities(C, ρ, n) = plane_waves(real_stiffness(C), ρ, n).velocity    ## qP, qS1, qS2
relative(A, B) = sqrt(sum(abs2, canonical_components(A - B)) / sum(abs2, canonical_components(B)))
const e₃ = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]

Case 1: aligned cracks ​

All the cracks have the normal . Under any load they are compressed alike and hold the same pressure: no fluid has a reason to move, and the sealed and the relaxed stiffnesses coincide. One family, at   and  :

julia
aligned = cracked_rock([e₃], 0.3, 1.0e-3)
relative(high(aligned), low(aligned))
1.9505753600866384e-16

The dry rock of this case has the anisotropy parameter of Thomsen   , from the compliance of eq. (2) of the article,      for thin cracks. Its ratio to the crack density, computed on the dry rock (the cracks of stiffness zero), against the two fractions:

julia
dry_aligned = homogenize(first(aligned), DiluteDual())
γ = thomsen_parameters(best_fit_ti(dry_aligned, e₃), average_density(first(aligned))).γ
(computed = γ / 0.3, from_eq_2 = 8(1 - ν₀) / (3(2 - ν₀)), printed_fraction = 8(1 - ν₀) / (3(1 - 2ν₀)))
(computed = 1.1239911946822831, from_eq_2 = 1.1252408477842004, printed_fraction = 4.231884057971015)

Eq. (14) of the article prints the fraction    and the approximate value . With   the fraction printed gives 4.2, and   , which eq. (2) gives, 1.125: the approximate value and the computation agree with the second form.

Case 2: randomly oriented cracks ​

The normals are drawn uniformly on the sphere. A finite set of families stands for them: the six axes of the regular icosahedron. Its twelve vertices form a spherical design of degree 5: the averages over them of the products of up to five components of are those of the uniform distribution, and among them the moments of eq. (16) of the article,  ,  ,  .

julia
const golden = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2
const icosahedron = normalize.([[0, 1, golden], [0, 1, -golden], [1, golden, 0], [1, -golden, 0], [golden, 0, 1], [-golden, 0, 1]])
moment(f) = sum(f, icosahedron) / length(icosahedron)
(n₁² = moment(n -> n[1]^2), n₁⁴ = moment(n -> n[1]^4), n₁²n₂² = moment(n -> n[1]^2 * n[2]^2))
(n₁² = 0.3333333333333333, n₁⁴ = 0.20000000000000004, n₁²n₂² = 0.06666666666666667)

A crack family adds to the compliance a tensor of degree four in its normal, so that six families give an isotropic rock. The distance of the two stiffnesses to their isotropic projection (best_fit_iso):

julia
random = cracked_rock(icosahedron, 0.3, 1.0e-3)
C_hf, C_lf = high(random), low(random)
(high = relative(C_hf, best_fit_iso(C_hf)), low = relative(C_lf, best_fit_iso(C_lf)))
(high = 3.334833620775775e-16, low = 3.071239268534955e-16)

The two limits in closed form ​

The article writes the extra compliance of the sealed cracks with the crack density tensors    and      (eqs. (3), (4), (9)):

the dry cracks having   . The relaxed compliance differs from it by eq. (10),        . With the moments of eq. (16),    and       . The bracket of the first term is  , and with   ,

since       has no spherical part. With    the first line is eq. (5), and is the shear modulus of the dry rock: a pressure uniform in all the cracks does not resist a shear.

julia
crack_δ(ξ) = π * ξ * E₀ * (1 / k_f - 1 / k₀) / (4(1 - ν₀^2))
function closed_form(ε, ξ)
    h = 32(1 - ν₀^2) / (3(2 - ν₀) * E₀)
    δ_f = crack_δ(ξ)
    ψ = (1 - ν₀ / 2) * δ_f / (1 + δ_f) - 1
    k_hf = inv(1 / k₀ + h * ε * (1 + ψ))
    μ_hf = inv(1 / μ₀ + 2h * ε * (1 / 3 + 2ψ / 15))
    μ_lf = inv(1 / μ_hf + 4h * ε * (1 - ν₀ / 2) / (15(1 + δ_f)))
    return (k_hf = k_hf, μ_hf = μ_hf, k_lf = k_hf, μ_lf = μ_lf)
end
moduli(C) = real.(bulk_shear(best_fit_iso(C)))
k_hf, μ_hf = moduli(C_hf)
k_lf, μ_lf = moduli(C_lf)
μ_dry = moduli(homogenize(first(random), DiluteDual()))[2]
ref = closed_form(0.3, 1.0e-3)
println("ε = 0.3, ξ = 1e-3     k^hf      k^lf      μ^hf      μ^lf      μ dry   (GPa)")
@printf "computed            %8.4f  %8.4f  %8.4f  %8.4f  %8.4f\n" k_hf k_lf μ_hf μ_lf μ_dry
@printf "closed form         %8.4f  %8.4f  %8.4f  %8.4f\n" ref.k_hf ref.k_lf ref.μ_hf ref.μ_lf
ε = 0.3, ξ = 1e-3     k^hf      k^lf      μ^hf      μ^lf      μ dry   (GPa)
computed             49.4478   49.4478   21.6103   19.3106   19.3106
closed form          49.4478   49.4478   21.6353   19.3290

The bulk modulus does not disperse: a hydrostatic stress compresses all the cracks alike, whatever their normals. The shear modulus does. The closed forms are those of infinitely thin cracks; the spheroids of the cell differ from them by terms of the order of .

Dispersion of the velocities ​

The article measures the dispersion of a wave by eq. (13),   , the velocity of the uncracked solid in the denominator. The rock being isotropic, any direction will do:

julia
const V_solid = velocities(C₀, ρ_s, e₃)
function dispersion(normals, ε, ξ, n = e₃)
    cell = cracked_rock(normals, ε, ξ)
    ρ = average_density(first(cell))
    return (velocities(high(cell), ρ, n) - velocities(low(cell), ρ, n)) ./ V_solid
end
ΔV = dispersion(icosahedron, 0.3, 1.0e-3)
(ΔV_P = ΔV[1], ΔV_S = ΔV[2], ratio = ΔV[1] / ΔV[2])
(ΔV_P = 0.018722631298354626, ΔV_S = 0.0484614387785782, ratio = 0.3863408056021387)

The article quotes an S-wave dispersion close to   at   and  , and   : the two numbers above. The same from the closed forms, with the velocities   and   of eq. (17):

julia
wave_speeds(k, μ) = (sqrt((k + 4μ / 3) / ρ_s), sqrt(μ / ρ_s))
function closed_dispersion(ε, ξ)
    m = closed_form(ε, ξ)
    return (wave_speeds(m.k_hf, m.μ_hf) .- wave_speeds(m.k_lf, m.μ_lf)) ./ wave_speeds(k₀, μ₀)
end
closed_dispersion(0.3, 1.0e-3)
(0.018765917405938838, 0.04855693996872711)

Against the crack density, for the two aspect ratios of the article, and against the aspect ratio at  ; the closed forms dashed:

julia
εs = range(0.01, quantity("crack_density_max"); length = 25)
ξs = 10 .^ range(log10(quantity("aspect_ratio_min")), log10(quantity("aspect_ratio_max")); length = 25)
panel(; kw...) = plot(; ylabel = "ΔV (%)", legend = :topleft, titlefontsize = 9, kw...)
by_density = map((quantity("aspect_ratio_a"), quantity("aspect_ratio_b"))) do ξ
    p = panel(; xlabel = "crack density ε", title = "random cracks, ξ = $ξ")
    computed = [dispersion(icosahedron, ε, ξ) for ε in εs]
    closed = [closed_dispersion(ε, ξ) for ε in εs]
    plot!(p, εs, 100 .* [getindex.(computed, 2) getindex.(computed, 1)]; lw = 2, color = [1 2], label = ["S" "P"])
    plot!(p, εs, 100 .* [last.(closed) first.(closed)]; lw = 1, ls = :dash, color = [1 2], label = ["closed forms" ""])
end
computed = [dispersion(icosahedron, 0.3, ξ) for ξ in ξs]
closed = [closed_dispersion(0.3, ξ) for ξ in ξs]
by_aspect = panel(; xlabel = "aspect ratio ξ", xscale = :log10, title = "random cracks, ε = 0.3", legend = :bottomleft)
plot!(by_aspect, ξs, 100 .* [getindex.(computed, 2) getindex.(computed, 1)]; lw = 2, color = [1 2], label = ["S" "P"])
plot!(by_aspect, ξs, 100 .* [last.(closed) first.(closed)]; lw = 1, ls = :dash, color = [1 2], label = ["closed forms" ""])
plot(by_density..., by_aspect; layout = (1, 3), size = (900, 300), left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm)

The dispersion is set by , which grows as . When   the fluid stiffens the sealed cracks almost as an incompressible one would, and the dispersion reaches a plateau; as grows, the sealed cracks soften toward the dry ones and the dispersion falls. The values of at the three aspect ratios of the article:

(0.024613928269638326, 0.24613928269638322, 2.4613928269638325)

Between the two limits ​

The article stops at the two limits. The exchange law of Jakobsen and Chapman gives the stiffness at every frequency: complex, its imaginary part being the energy the flow dissipates. For a time dependence , a modulus    gives a plane wave of wavenumber , hence the phase velocity and the inverse quality factor

with   for the S waves and    for the P waves of the isotropic rock. At   and  :

julia
ωτs = 10 .^ range(-4, 2; length = 121)
ρ_random = average_density(first(random))
spectrum = map(ωτs) do ωτ
    k, μ = bulk_shear(best_fit_iso(saturated(random..., ωτ)))
    (S = μ, P = k + 4μ / 3)
end
phase_velocity(M) = 1 / real(sqrt(ρ_random / M))
inverse_Q(M) = imag(M) / real(M)
V_S, V_P = phase_velocity.(getfield.(spectrum, :S)), phase_velocity.(getfield.(spectrum, :P))
Q_S, Q_P = inverse_Q.(getfield.(spectrum, :S)), inverse_Q.(getfield.(spectrum, :P))
julia
velocity_panel = plot(
    ωτs, [V_S ./ V_S[1] V_P ./ V_P[1]]; xscale = :log10, lw = 2, label = ["S" "P"], legend = :topleft,
    xlabel = "ωτ", ylabel = "V / V(ωτ → 0)", title = "phase velocity", titlefontsize = 9
)
attenuation_panel = plot(
    ωτs, 100 .* [Q_S Q_P]; xscale = :log10, lw = 2, label = ["S" "P"], legend = :topleft,
    xlabel = "ωτ", ylabel = "Q⁻¹ (%)", title = "attenuation", titlefontsize = 9
)
plot(velocity_panel, attenuation_panel; layout = (1, 2), size = (760, 300), left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm)

The velocity climbs from the relaxed to the sealed value over two decades, and the attenuation peaks in between, at of a few hundredths rather than one. The rise of the velocities over the whole range is the dispersion of the previous section, up to its denominator:

julia
(S = V_S[end] / V_S[1] - 1, P = V_P[end] / V_P[1] - 1)
(S = 0.05786937541738135, P = 0.020184595281983464)

A single relaxation ​

Where the peak sits follows from the non-interacting approximation, in which each family sees the remote stress alone. The volume strain of a crack of family whose fluid is at the pressure is that of the dry crack under , plus that of the crack under the pressure in an unloaded solid. The latter is the sum of the uniform stress in the solid and in the crack, and of the dry crack under the remote stress . With the compressibility of the dry crack (its volume strain per unit confining pressure) and   that of the solid,

where depends on the normal of the family and on its shape only. With  , the exchange law of Levin's theorem, §5,     and       , gives

The families have one shape and one volume fraction, and the conservation   makes the mean of the . The mean of the equation over the families gives     at every frequency: the common pressure of the relaxed state. Then

being the pressure of the sealed crack. The macroscopic strain is linear in and in the pressures, hence a single relaxation:

The shear compliance follows the same law, so that     , largest at  , where it equals  . A thin crack is far more compliant than the fluid it holds,  : its pressure moves with little fluid, and the relaxation takes place well below  . In terms of the parameter of the previous section,   , the relaxation is at    .

is read on the strain concentration tensor of a dry family, gradient_flux_concentration, which gives per unit remote stress:

julia
const 𝟏 = TensISO{3}(1.0)
dry_cell = first(cracked_rock([e₃], 0.3, 1.0e-3))
C_p = 𝟏 ⊡ gradient_flux_concentration(concentration_tensors(dry_cell, DiluteDual()), :cracks1) ⊡ 𝟏
κ, C_s = 1 / k_f, 1 / k₀
ωτ_relax = κ / (C_p + κ - C_s)
(C_p = C_p, ωτ_relax = ωτ_relax, thin_cracks = crack_δ(1.0e-3) / (1 + crack_δ(1.0e-3)))
(C_p = 16.864294656381983, ωτ_relax = 0.02516195818184448, thin_cracks = 0.02402263681034102)

The stiffness of squirt_flow against the single relaxation, over the whole range of frequencies, and the peak of :

julia
debye(ωτ) = (Ω = ωτ / ωτ_relax; inv(C_lf) + (inv(C_hf) - inv(C_lf)) * (im * Ω / (1 + im * Ω)))
largest_gap = maximum(relative(inv(saturated(random..., ωτ)), debye(ωτ)) for ωτ in ωτs)
ωτ_peak = ωτ_relax * sqrt(μ_hf / μ_lf)
μ_peak = bulk_shear(best_fit_iso(saturated(random..., ωτ_peak)))[2]
(largest_gap = largest_gap, ωτ_peak = ωτ_peak, Q⁻¹ = inverse_Q(μ_peak), closed_form = (μ_hf - μ_lf) / (2sqrt(μ_hf * μ_lf)))
(largest_gap = 4.411426985701448e-14, ωτ_peak = 0.02661808686400653, Q⁻¹ = 0.056287363984448856, closed_form = 0.056287363984441056)

Case 3: vertical cracks ​

The normals now lie in the horizontal plane, uniformly in azimuth. Six families, at the azimuths , give the same averages of the products of up to four components of as the uniform distribution, and the rock is transversely isotropic about :

julia
const vertical = [[cos(k * π / 6), sin(k * π / 6), 0.0] for k in 0:5]
upright = cracked_rock(vertical, 0.3, 1.0e-3)
C_up_hf, C_up_lf = high(upright), low(upright)
(high = relative(C_up_hf, best_fit_ti(C_up_hf, e₃)), low = relative(C_up_lf, best_fit_ti(C_up_lf, e₃)))
(high = 1.7383922495408595e-16, low = 1.9096464427787015e-16)

A wave traveling in the plane at the angle from the vertical has a P wave and two S waves: the SH wave polarized along , normal to that plane, and the SV wave polarized in it. They are told apart by their polarizations:

julia
function upright_waves(C, ρ, θ)
    w = plane_waves(real_stiffness(C), ρ, [sin(θ), 0.0, cos(θ)])
    sh = abs(w.polarization[2, 2]) > abs(w.polarization[2, 3]) ? 2 : 3    ## the S wave polarized along e₂
    return (P = w.velocity[1], SH = w.velocity[sh], SV = w.velocity[5 - sh])
end
ρ_upright = average_density(first(upright))
println("direction          ΔV_P (%)  ΔV_SH (%)  ΔV_SV (%)")
for (name, θ) in (("vertical", 0.0), ("45°", π / 4), ("horizontal", π / 2))
    hf, lf = upright_waves(C_up_hf, ρ_upright, θ), upright_waves(C_up_lf, ρ_upright, θ)
    @printf "%-17s %8.3f   %8.3f   %8.3f\n" name 100 * (hf.P - lf.P) / V_solid[1] 100 * (hf.SH - lf.SH) / V_solid[2] 100 * (hf.SV - lf.SV) / V_solid[2]
end
direction          ΔV_P (%)  ΔV_SH (%)  ΔV_SV (%)
vertical             0.000      0.000      0.000
45°                  0.491      3.844      1.864
horizontal           2.181      7.888      0.000

The vertical P wave loads every vertical crack with the same normal stress, and its pressure is the same in all of them: no dispersion. The horizontal SV wave, polarized along , applies the shear stress , whose traction on a vertical crack lies in its plane: no pressure at all. The horizontal SH wave applies , which compresses the cracks of one diagonal and opens those of the other: the largest pressure differences, and the largest dispersion. The velocities of the P and SH waves against the direction of propagation, sealed and relaxed:

julia
θs = range(0, π / 2; length = 91)
V_P_hf = [upright_waves(C_up_hf, ρ_upright, θ).P for θ in θs]
V_P_lf = [upright_waves(C_up_lf, ρ_upright, θ).P for θ in θs]
V_SH_hf = [upright_waves(C_up_hf, ρ_upright, θ).SH for θ in θs]
V_SH_lf = [upright_waves(C_up_lf, ρ_upright, θ).SH for θ in θs]
plot(
    plot(
        rad2deg.(θs), [V_P_hf V_P_lf]; lw = 2, ls = [:solid :dash], label = ["sealed (hf)" "relaxed (lf)"],
        xlabel = "θ from the vertical (degrees)", ylabel = "V_P (km/s)", title = "P wave", titlefontsize = 9, xticks = 0:15:90
    ),
    plot(
        rad2deg.(θs), [V_SH_hf V_SH_lf]; lw = 2, ls = [:solid :dash], label = ["sealed (hf)" "relaxed (lf)"],
        xlabel = "θ from the vertical (degrees)", ylabel = "V_SH (km/s)", title = "SH wave", titlefontsize = 9, xticks = 0:15:90
    ); layout = (1, 2), size = (760, 300), left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm
)

Case 3 mixes the two previous ones: anisotropic like case 1, dispersive like case 2, and the dispersion itself depends on the direction.
